The Cursor security incident shows why securing coding agent traces matters

Here’s how the attacker reached the Claude Code extension:

- Obtained a Cursor credential exposed through Fireworks AI

- Accessed historical agent traces containing unredacted API keys

- Used those keys to access Cursor’s internal systems

- Compromised the extension distribution process and shipped a malicious Claude Code extension with an SSH backdoor

The problem wasn’t storing historical traces. It was failing to properly secure them and protect the secrets they contained

Bug bounty tip: read the skill before you install it.

Skills and MCP servers are the new browser extensions. Everyone installs them, nobody opens the file.

Some numbers.

One audit of a public skill marketplace found 341 malicious skills. That was about 12% of everything listed.

A fake MCP server on npm copied a real one and worked fine for 15 versions. Then one added line started sending a copy of every email to the attacker. About 1,600 downloads before anyone noticed.

A research paper on malicious skills is titled "Do Not Mention This to the User." That tells you what they found inside.

Your agent runs with your session, your tokens and your target notes. So before you install anything, check:

- Who published it, and is it the real one or a lookalike name
- What commands it runs
- Where it sends data
- Any instruction that has nothing to do with what the skill is for

Then pin the version. The safe one today can change tomorrow.

Five minutes of reading. Or a stranger steers your agent.

I would not call an agent session isolated if its files still land in a shared bucket.

AWS made the next generation of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime the default on Nov 12. I have not used it. This is from their blog and the what's-new note, not a hands-on test.

https://t.co/MRn5ZQMcsY

https://t.co/Hvt3rTtP7N

The core guarantee they keep is that every session runs in its own Firecracker microVM, with its own identity, policy, and audit trail. New sessions start from a snapshot of the initialized agent, scale up to 8 vCPUs and 32 GB, and an idle agent scales to zero. On a 2 GB image, they report starts under 2 seconds at P75, down from 29.7 seconds.

The part I would actually watch is the data boundary. They say isolation that stops at compute is only half a boundary, and sessions can now mount a filesystem such as an S3 bucket inside that trust boundary. The tighter fix they describe, binding each session to its own storage folder with session-labeled credentials, is scheduled for re:Invent and is not in this release.

If I were putting a long-running agent on this runtime, I would keep one user's files out of a shared bucket until that per-session scoping ships.

The most embarrassing outage of the year is an expired TLS certificate.

Nothing was deployed and no code changed. One day the site just shows a browser warning, and every API call between your services fails with a handshake error.

It keeps happening because certificates expire quietly. Someone bought one for a year, set a calendar reminder, and then left the company.

How to stop it:

- Automate issuance and renewal: Let's Encrypt with certbot, cert-manager on Kubernetes, or ACM on AWS
- Alert on days until expiry, at 30, 14, and 7 days, not just on failure
- Monitor the certificate your endpoint actually serves, not the one in your config. A renewed cert that was never reloaded is still expired.
- Don't forget internal certs: mTLS between services, databases, and load balancers
- Keep an inventory of every cert and who owns it

If renewal depends on a human remembering, it will eventually fail.

Automate anything that expires.

Microsoft 365 went down for over a day. 
Here's what we know so far.

1. Thursday, 12 Nov: Outlook, Exchange Online and Teams start failing
Microsoft said failed server health checks disrupted Outlook and other Microsoft 365 services.

2. First diagnosis: "elevated load"
Microsoft first thought infrastructure was under elevated load across multiple regions, and suspected a traffic spike. 
As a first containment step, it started redistributing connection traffic across its worldwide infrastructure. That didn't help.

3. Diagnosis revised
Microsoft clarified the load was not from a traffic increase, but from a large number of servers becoming unexpectedly unavailable. It began restarting servers that were failing health checks and reviewing recent changes.

4. Focus shifts to one component
Microsoft said a process that establishes secure connections was becoming overwhelmed, causing affected servers to stop handling requests. 
The first containment attempt failed and the diagnosis changed twice, which stretched the outage past a day.

5. Friday: Microsoft names a cause
Microsoft apologised and said the incident was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change. It also said there was no evidence of malicious activity.

6. Saturday: recovery
Mailbox access is restored, though residual delays are possible and the root-cause report is still to come.
Why it happened (what's confirmed)

A network capacity upgrade, followed by a later network change
Servers failed health checks and the secure-connection process was overwhelmed

Microsoft's own explanation shifted over time, which delayed the fix
The Verge reported that sources link it to Azure Virtual Network config changes. That's unconfirmed.

-->> How it was resolved
Traffic redistribution failed, then Microsoft restarted unhealthy servers and traced the fault to the health-processing component. It then fixed the underlying network issue. The full detail is still pending.
Takeaways for engineers

A wrong first diagnosis can cost hours, so check recent changes early

Failed health checks can take out healthy capacity
Capacity upgrades and network changes need the same rollout discipline as code

I'll update this once the post-incident report lands.

Claude CodeやCursorにコーディングを任せられるようになった分、人間が判断しないといけないのは、設計のレイヤーになってきた気がする

AIにコーディングを任せられるようになって、書く時間は減ったけど、判断する場面はむしろ増えた

「データはSQLとNoSQLどっちで持つ？」
「一覧が重いけど、キャッシュはどこに置く？」
「リアルタイムの通知はWebSocketでいい？」

AIはどれもそれっぽく答えてくれるけど、どれを採るかは結局人間が決めることになる

なので設計を学び直したいって人も多いと思うけど、「system-design 」は最高の教材だと思う

・ネットワークの土台から、データベース、サービスの分け方まで順番に読める
・WhatsApp、Twitter、Netflix、Uberなどの、実在の有名サービスを設計する演習までついてる
・設計の主な選択肢には、得意と不得意がセットで書いてある

なぜこの設計がこの要件に効くのかまでしっかり学べるから、設計の正解を覚えるのではなくて、考える際の選択肢を色々増やせる感じでめちゃいい

the key insight i learned from @mgarimella was to design goals around what you can give feedback on more easily

feedback (used to align the agent with your mental model of what it should do) is the hardest thing to extract from users

so the more you can design your system (ui, goals, etc) around making that easy to do - the better!
